Sampling (Sect 1.2)

Collecting Data

  • The conclusions (inferences) that can be made using data are determined by how the data was collected.
    • Sampling: make conclusions about populations
    • Experiments: investigate causality by manipulating one or more variables
    • Observational Studies: exploring associations between variables by observing (not manipulating) variables

Measurements of penguins at Palmer Station, Antarctica to study sexual dimorphism

  • Three species: Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo
  • Three islands: Biscoe, Dream, Torgersen
  • Length measurements in mm, mass in g

Carleton’s Mission Statement

Activity:

  • Question: What is the average word length?
  • Task: Select a sample of 10 words to estimate average word length of entire statement

Determine the following:

  1. Population? (describe cases of interest)
  2. Sample?
  3. Pick your sample
  4. Variable measured?
  5. Compute average word length

Results

  1. Population = all words in statement

    • The (unknown) average word length is an example of a population parameter.
    • Number of cases: number of words in the statement

  2. Sample = 10 samples words

  3. Is your sample the same as your neighbor’s sample?

  4. Variable measured = length of word

  5. Is your sample average the same as your neighbor’s?

    • Your sample average word length is an example of a sample statistic.

Results

  • Actual average:

    5.76 letters

  • People are (usually) TERRIBLE at selecting a good sample, even when explicitly trying to avoid sampling bias!

Random Sample- Carleton Mission

  • Let’s use R to find true random samples of 10 words

Analysis Steps:

  1. Population: Enumerate all 229 words in the Mission Statement (called a sampling frame)

  2. Sample: Use technology to pick 10 random numbers between 1 and 229 (samp_ind <- sample(1:229, size = 10))

    • Units: “dedicated” “seeks” “valued” “and” “welcoming” “and” “and” “ethical” “as” “neighbors”

  3. Calculate the average number of letters in the words corresponding to your random numbers

    • 9 5 6 3 9 3 3 7 2 9
    • 5.6 letters

Sampling

Key idea: want sample to be representative of population

Sampling bias: sampling mechanism causes systematic difference from the population

A simple random sample (SRS) avoids sampling bias

  • Each population member is equally likely to be chosen in the sample

Realities of SRS

Obstacles:

  1. Need a list of all population members
  2. Need a method to measure any population member
    • Nonresponse bias: nonresponders may be systematically different from responders

In practice, obtaining a representative sample takes care

Other Sources of Bias

For human data especially:

  • Question wording/context/framing
  • Dishonesty
  • Nonresponse

In general,

  • instrument calibration
  • communication in the sample

Summary

  • Statisticians use data to learn about things / quantify uncertainty
  • Data are (often) comprised of variables measured on cases
  • The population is the thing you want to learn about
  • The sample comes from the population
  • A representative sample ensures valid statistical inference
  • Simple random sampling can make a representative sample

Activity

Running Commands

In the Console tab enter the commands (hit Enter after each line)

  • ‘#’ is the start of a comment
  • Like a note, not actually used by R
log(2^2) # basic arithmetic (log is ln)
1:5 # vectors of numbers 1 thru 5
c(3,1,2) # c = concatenate
x <- 10:1 # assignment
x^2 # arithmetic on vectors
x[c(2,4)] # subsetting

Here’s what you should actually expect to see:

[1] 1 2 3 4 5
> c(3,1,2) # c = concatenate
[1] 3 1 2
> x <- 10:1 # assignment
> x^2 # arithmetic on vectors
[1] 100 81 64 49 36 25 16 9 4 1
> x[c(2,4)] # subsetting
[1] 9 7

  • Seeing your objects: type ls() or look in the Environment tab
  • Objects have different types
class(x) #reveals the class of the object

Common types: int, numeric, factor, character, data.frame, lm

R Markdown

R Markdown

  • An R Markdown (.Rmd) file contains the commands and written analysis used to complete a data analysis for an assignment or report.
  • The .Rmd file is compiled (“knit”) to generate an HTML, PDF, or Word document with written analysis, R commands and output.
  • Write-up homework and reports in Markdown docs
  • Start simple: use .Rmd templates, modify in small steps and knit often!

R Markdown

3 Components

  1. Header: info like the title, author, and output type preferences
  2. Written analysis: You can create formatting details like bold words, lists, section labels, latex equations, etc to your final pdf/word/html document.
  3. R chunks: R commands that you want evaluated.

After knitting the file, a pdf/html/Word file will be created in the same folder as the .Rmd

Tips

  • When you knit, R starts from scratch
  • This means you must have all commands in your .Rmd for your file to knit correctly. Make sure your .Rmd has:
    • a data loading command
    • any package loading library command

Download day02_c1_2SamplingExamples.Rmd from Moodle and upload to Maize
